newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan PM Hashimoto sets numerical targets for cuts.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM Hashimoto sets numerical targets for cuts.

text.p: A Japanese government panel headed by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto released a report on Tuesday seeking drastic cuts in government spending and laying out the groundwork for an overhaul of Japan's debt-ridden finances.

The report set out specific numerical targets for the proposed cuts in many areas traditionally considered as "sanctuaries", such as public works, defence and agricultural assistance with the aim of keeping next fiscal year's general expenditures 0.5 percent below this year's levels.

Hashimoto set fiscal reform as one of his top policy goals and formed the panel in January to live up to his pledge of slashing the government deficit to three percent or less of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2003.
Japan's fiscal deficit for calendar 1997 is forecast at about 6.3 percent of gross domestic product, one of the highest levels among major industrialised countries.

Hashimoto plans for the report to receive cabinet approval today and the government will then incorporate it into a fiscal reform law, which it aims to submit to an extraordinary session of parliament, expected to convene in the autumn.
The panel is comprised of government ministers and key ruling party officials.
The report called for cuts in the following areas:

- Public works. Spending should be decreased by at least seven percent in the 1998/99 fiscal year. Annual spending should also be decreased by extending the length of a five-year public spending plan by three years while keeping the total amount of spending in the plan unchanged.
- Defence spending. Spending for the 1998/99 year should be limited to 1997/98 levels or less. In addition, spending allotted to a five-year plan should be cut by 920 billion yen.
- Overseas aid. Spending for the 1998/99 year should be decreased by at least 10 percent. Medium-term targets for Official Development Assistance (ODA) should be abolished.
- Social welfare. Growth in social welfare spending should be limited to 300 billion yen or less in the 1998/99 year.

- Agriculture. Assistance to farmers faced with competition from imports as a result of the Uruguay Round agreement of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade should be scaled back. This should be achieved by extending the six-year assistance plan by two years while keeping the total amount of assistance unchanged.
